title: Genetics: Mendel's Laws and Sex-Linked Inheritance
tagline: Monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, sex determination, and the inheritance of haemophilia and colour blindness.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Heredity explains why offspring resemble their parents while never being identical. This chapter works through Mendel's experiments with peas, from which two laws were generalised — the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment — and the crosses that demonstrate them: monohybrid (one character, 3:1 ratio) and dihybrid (two characters, 9:3:3:1 ratio), with test crosses used to reveal unknown genotypes. The chapter then turns to sex determination, where the chromosomes received from each parent decide the sex of the offspring, and to sex-linked inheritance, which explains why conditions such as colour blindness and haemophilia appear mostly in males.

blocks.text: Mendel chose peas because they self-pollinate naturally, have true-breeding varieties and show clear either-or characters. Crossing tall and dwarf plants gave an F1 generation that was all tall — one factor had masked the other. Letting the F1 self-pollinate produced an F2 generation of roughly three tall to one dwarf, showing that the dwarf factor had not been lost but merely hidden. From such results Mendel proposed two laws. The law of segregation states that the two factors for a character separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one factor for that character. The law of independent assortment states that the factors for different characters separate independently of one another — true only for genes on different chromosomes, which is why dihybrid crosses give the 9:3:3:1 ratio.

items.meaning: A unit of inheritance that controls a particular characteristic; an alternative form is an allele.
The allele expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy is present (written with a capital letter, e.g. T).
The allele expressed only in homozygous condition (written lowercase, e.g. t); masked by a dominant allele in heterozygotes.
The genetic constitution, e.g. TT, Tt or tt.
The observable characteristic, e.g. tall or dwarf.
Two identical alleles / two different alleles for a character.

items: F1 generation shows only the dominant character; the recessive reappears in F2.
Monohybrid cross: Tt x Tt gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypes and 1:2:1 genotypes.
Test cross: crossing an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive reveals the unknown by its offspring ratios.
Law of segregation: allele pairs separate during gametogenesis so each gamete receives one allele.
Law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes segregate independently — reflected in the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio.
Dominance does not mean the recessive allele is 'weaker' — it is simply unexpressed when a dominant allele is present.

items.text: Monohybrid: Tt x Tt gives gametes T and t from each parent; offspring TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1, phenotype 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
items.note: The genotypic 1:2:1 underlies the phenotypic 3:1 — show both when asked.

items.text: Test cross: unknown tall pea plant x tt. If all offspring are tall, the parent was TT; if about half are dwarf, it was Tt.
items.note: The recessive tester cannot mask anything, so the unknown's alleles show directly.

items.text: Dihybrid: RrYy x RrYy gives 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green.
items.note: Each character separately behaves as a 3:1 monohybrid; multiplying the probabilities gives 9:3:3:1.

blocks.text: In humans, sex is decided by the twenty-third pair of chromosomes — the sex chromosomes, written X and Y. A female is 44 + XX and can produce only X-bearing eggs. A male is 44 + XY and produces half X-bearing and half Y-bearing sperm. Fertilisation by an X sperm gives 44 + XX (a female); by a Y sperm gives 44 + XY (a male). Since the mother always contributes an X, it is the father's sperm that determines the sex of the child. Meiosis is what makes the 50:50 sperm ratio possible: the X and Y chromosomes separate as a homologous pair during meiosis I.

items: Human somatic cells: 44 autosomes + 2 sex chromosomes; gametes carry 23.
Eggs: all 22 + X; sperm: 22 + X or 22 + Y in equal proportions.
The sperm entering the egg decides the sex — 50:50 chance each pregnancy.
In the XO system of grasshoppers, females are XX and males X0 — the male-heterogametic pattern again.

items.text: Punnett square: X egg x Y sperm gives XX daughter; X egg x X sperm gives XX daughter — equal halves.
items.note: Showing the square demonstrates why blaming the mother for a child's sex is biologically wrong.

items.text: Colour-blind father (XcY) and normal mother (XX): all sons normal, all daughters carriers (XcX).
items.note: Sons receive their only X from the mother — the route by which X-linked traits pass.

learn.title: Sex-linked inheritance: haemophilia and colour blindness

blocks.text: Genes carried on the X chromosome show sex-linked inheritance because males have only one X and therefore only one copy of every X-linked gene, while females have two copies and must be homozygous to express a recessive X-linked condition. Red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are both recessive X-linked traits. A colour-blind male passes his X chromosome to all his daughters, making them at least carriers, but never to his sons. A carrier mother passes the affected X to half her sons, of whom about half express the condition — which is why these conditions are far more common in males. A female expresses the condition only if her father is affected and her mother is a carrier or affected, a much rarer combination.

items: X-linked recessive: males need one affected X to show the trait; females need two.
Colour blindness: inability to distinguish red and green; tested with Ishihara plates.
Haemophilia: blood lacks clotting factor, so bleeding continues; controlled but not cured.
Criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter to grandson — the trait skips generations through carrier females.
A colour-blind daughter must have an affected father and at least a carrier mother.
Carriers are phenotypically normal but can pass the allele on.

items.text: Normal carrier mother (XXc) x normal father (XY): half the sons colour-blind, half normal; all daughters phenotypically normal.
items.note: The ratio among sons is 1:1 — every son gets his only X from the mother.

items.text: Colour-blind father x homozygous normal mother: daughters are all carriers, sons all normal.
items.note: Fathers cannot pass X-linked traits to sons — sons get their Y from the father.

items.text: Haemophilia in royal families spread through carrier queens to sons across Europe.
items.note: A historical example of criss-cross inheritance.

items.meaning: A gene located on a sex chromosome, most commonly the X.
A female with one copy of a recessive X-linked allele who does not express it.
Recessive X-linked inability to discriminate red and green wavelengths.
Recessive X-linked disorder in which blood fails to clot normally.
Passage of a trait from father through carrier daughter to grandson.

keyPoints: Mendel's law of segregation: allele pairs separate during gamete formation, one allele per gamete.
Mendel's law of independent assortment: alleles of different characters segregate independently.
Monohybrid F2: 3:1 phenotype ratio; 1:2:1 genotype ratio.
Dihybrid F2: 9:3:3:1 for two independent characters.
Test cross = unknown x homozygous recessive, used to determine genotype.
Human sex chromosomes: female 44 + XX, male 44 + XY; the father determines the sex.
Colour blindness and haemophilia are recessive X-linked traits, commoner in males.
A male passes his X chromosome to all his daughters and none of his sons.
A female expresses an X-linked recessive condition only when homozygous.
examFocus: Cross questions need the full working: parents, gametes, Punnett square, then BOTH ratios — answers without the square lose method marks.
For sex-linked questions write the alleles on the X (Xc for colour blindness) and never on the Y — most lost marks come from placing the gene on the Y.
'Why is colour blindness commoner in males?' expects one-copy expression in XY versus two copies required in XX.
Test-cross answers must state the two possible offspring patterns and what each implies about the unknown genotype.

vocabulary.meaning: Expressed with one copy / expressed only with two copies.
Cross with a homozygous recessive to reveal an unknown genotype.
Heterozygote with a recessive allele not expressed in the phenotype.
Inherited via a gene on a sex chromosome (usually X).

questions.prompt: A monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of:
questions.explanation: Tt x Tt gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypes; 1:2:1 is the genotypic ratio and 9:3:3:1 belongs to dihybrid crosses.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 1:2:1 — that ratio counts genotypes, not visible phenotypes.

questions.prompt: The sex of a human child is determined by:
questions.explanation: Eggs always carry X; sperm carry X or Y in equal numbers. An X sperm gives a daughter (XX) and a Y sperm a son (XY).
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the mother decides — she has no Y chromosome to contribute.

questions.explanation: It lies on the X chromosome and is expressed only when no normal allele is present — in males (single X) or homozygous females.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Y-linked — Y-linked traits pass father to son, which colour blindness does not do.

questions.prompt: A colour-blind man and a homozygous normal woman have children. Their sons will be:
questions.explanation: Sons receive their only X from the mother, who gives a normal X; the father's X goes to daughters, who become carriers.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting sons to inherit the father's X — males inherit their X exclusively from the mother.

questions.prompt: Mendel's law of independent assortment is demonstrated by:
questions.explanation: Only a cross following two characters at once can show that the alleles segregate independently, giving 9:3:3:1.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the test cross, which reveals genotype but says nothing about independent assortment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the F2 genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross is ________, and the phenotypic ratio is ________.
questions.explanation: TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1 produces 3 dominant-phenotype to 1 recessive-phenotype because Tt looks like TT.
questions.commonMistake: Writing the phenotypic ratio first without recognising that heterozygotes merge into the dominant class.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a haemophilia-carrying mother (XhX) and a normal father (XY) have a probability of ________ that their son is haemophilic, and their daughters are all ________.
questions.answer: one half (50 per cent); phenotypically normal (at least carriers)
questions.explanation: Half the sons receive Xh and express the condition; daughters receive a normal X from the father so none expresses it, though half become carriers.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming daughters are unaffected AND cannot carry — they can carry and pass it on.

questions.prompt: State Mendel's two laws and give the offspring ratio that illustrates each.
questions.answer: Law of segregation: the two factors (alleles) for a character separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one — illustrated by the monohybrid F2 ratios of 3:1 (phenotype) and 1:2:1 (genotype). Law of independent assortment: factors for different characters separate independently of one another — illustrated by the dihybrid F2 ratio of 9:3:3:1.
questions.explanation: Each law needs both the statement and its numerical demonstration; ratios alone or statements alone earn only partial marks.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing 9:3:3:1 to the law of segregation — that ratio requires two characters assorting independently.

questions.prompt: What is a test cross, and how does it distinguish a homozygous dominant from a heterozygous individual?
questions.answer: A test cross is a mating between the individual of unknown genotype and a homozygous recessive tester. The recessive parent can contribute only recessive alleles, so the offspring phenotype directly reflects the unknown's gametes. If all offspring show the dominant phenotype, the unknown is homozygous dominant (TT x tt -> all Tt). If about half show the recessive phenotype, the unknown is heterozygous (Tt x tt -> 1 Tt : 1 tt).
questions.explanation: The tester's alleles cannot mask anything, so the offspring ratio maps one-to-one onto the unknown's genotype.
questions.commonMistake: Describing it as a 'back cross' — a back cross is any cross to a parent; a test cross specifically uses the homozygous recessive.

questions.prompt: Explain why red-green colour blindness is much more common in males than in females.
questions.answer: The allele is recessive and carried on the X chromosome. Males are XY, so they have only one X: a single colour-blind allele on that X is expressed, with no second X to provide a normal copy. Females are XX and need two copies of the recessive allele — one from each parent — to express it; with one copy they are unaffected carriers. Since a colour-blind allele is rare in the population, the chance of a female inheriting two is far lower than a male inheriting one, so males are far more frequently affected.
questions.explanation: The answer combines hemizygosity in males with the double-dose requirement in females.
questions.commonMistake: Saying males are 'weaker' or that the gene is on the Y — the mechanism is the single X, and Y-linkage would make it father-to-son only.

questions.prompt: A woman is a carrier for colour blindness (XCXc) and a normal man (XCY) have children. Give the Punnett square, and state the phenotype of each class of offspring with probabilities.
questions.answer: Gametes: mother gives XC and Xc; father gives XC and Y. Offspring: XCXC — normal daughter (25 per cent); XCXc — carrier daughter, phenotypically normal (25 per cent); XCY — normal son (25 per cent); XcY — colour-blind son (25 per cent). Overall: all children are phenotypically normal except the colour-blind sons, who are one quarter of all children and one half of the sons.
questions.explanation: The square shows both X chromosomes of the mother segregating independently; only sons can express the single paternal-Y combination with the maternal Xc.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that half the sons are affected — writing 'all normal' because daughters mask the trait.

questions.prompt: Why can a normal woman give birth to a colour-blind son and a colour-blind daughter, and what must the father be in each case?
questions.answer: A phenotypically normal woman can be a carrier (XCXc). To have a colour-blind son (XcY) she must pass Xc and the father must contribute Y — the father may be normal (XCY) or colour blind (XcY). To have a colour-blind daughter (XcXc) the daughter must receive Xc from BOTH parents, so the father must be colour blind (XcY) and the mother must have passed her Xc. Thus the rarer daughter requires an affected father, while the son requires only a carrier mother.
questions.explanation: The daughter's double requirement versus the son's single copy is the heart of X-linked inheritance probabilities.
questions.commonMistake: Overlooking that a normal-phenotype mother can carry the allele — 'normal' phenotype does not mean homozygous normal.
